title: thenApply vs thenApplyAsync: which thread runs the callback, when to use each
keyPoints: thenApply runs the callback on the thread that completed the previous stage (or the caller if already done).
thenApplyAsync submits the callback to an Executor, guaranteeing a thread switch.
Use thenApply for cheap transforms like parseInt or string formatting (no thread switch overhead).
Use thenApplyAsync for blocking or heavy work so you do not tie up the completing thread.
Blocking in a non-async stage on ForkJoinPool starves all other CompletableFutures in the JVM.
Always pass a dedicated IO pool to thenApplyAsync for blocking calls: thenApplyAsync(fn, ioPool).

s1_definition.oneliner: thenApply runs the callback on the completing thread (cheap and fast), while thenApplyAsync runs it on a pool thread (necessary for blocking or heavy work to avoid starving the completing thread).
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Non-async (thenApply)** – the callback runs on the thread that completed the previous stage, or on the caller's thread if the CF was already done; no thread switch overhead.
- **Async (thenApplyAsync)** – the callback is submitted to an Executor (default: ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), or custom); guaranteed thread switch.
- **Danger** – blocking work in a non-async stage ties up the completing thread, which may be a ForkJoinPool worker, starving all other futures.
- **Rule** – non-async for cheap transforms (parseInt, multiply, format); async with dedicated executor for blocking or CPU-heavy work.
- **Custom pool** – `thenApplyAsync(fn, ioPool)` runs the callback on a dedicated IO pool, keeping ForkJoinPool free.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India: thenApply is the delivery person who brought the bank statement also calculating the interest right at the door. If it is quick math, that is fine. If it is a five-minute audit, the delivery person is stuck at the door and cannot deliver other statements. thenApplyAsync is having a separate accountant do the calculation, so the delivery person continues delivering immediately.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  thenApply (no thread switch)
  ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐
  │ supplyAsync   │────▶│ thenApply    │
  │ FJP-thread-1  │     │ FJP-thread-1 │  ← same thread!
  └──────────────┘     └──────────────┘

  thenApplyAsync (thread switch)
  ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐
  │ supplyAsync   │────▶│ thenApplyAsync│
  │ FJP-thread-1  │     │ ioPool-5     │  ← different thread!
  └──────────────┘     └──────────────┘
  FJP-thread-1 freed immediately
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The non-async methods (thenApply, thenAccept, thenCombine) run the callback on the thread that completed the previous stage. This is fast for cheap transforms because there is no thread switch overhead. The async variants (thenApplyAsync, thenAcceptAsync) submit the callback to an executor, guaranteeing a thread switch and freeing the completing thread immediately.

The critical rule: never do blocking or heavy work in a non-async stage. ForkJoinPool.commonPool() has only cores - 1 threads. Blocking all of them stalls every CompletableFuture in the JVM. Use thenApplyAsync(fn, dedicatedIoPool) for database calls, HTTP requests, and file operations. Use thenApplyAsync(fn, cpuPool) for encryption and sorting.

At National Bank of India, a credit bureau API call (500ms blocking) was in a thenApply stage. It stalled all ForkJoinPool threads, delaying balance lookups by 500ms. Switching to thenApplyAsync with a dedicated IO pool freed the FJP for other work.

Remember one sentence: use thenApply for cheap transforms, thenApplyAsync with a dedicated pool for anything that blocks.
